title: Barney Bigard learning clarinet; violin in old Dixieland; the one-beat style
summary: A long account of how Barney learned from Papa Tio and Lorenzo Tio, swapped lessons with Albert Nicholas, went to Chicago and joined Duke Ellington; also how violinists played and why Dixieland is a one-beat music.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone

We'd go up to see Barney at the theater and he told us a little bit about T.O. too, how he studied with T.O. and I noticed that Barney uses both lips on the cupboard over his teeth and not very many people here do that anymore. Do you know that the T.O.s ever teach him that? I forget. I don't know if he told me if T.O. taught him. Well, I'll tell you, it was not T.O. that taught him the clarinet and the way of speaking. T.O.'s grandfather is the one that taught him. Was that Papa or Louis? Papa T.O. Papa T.O. and after Papa T.O. taking and he told Barney, he says, Barney, I can't teach you anymore. He says, you know as much as me. He said, but go to Lorenzo and he's finished teaching. When Barney went back to Lorenzo, Lorenzo told Barney, there's nothing I can't do for you, you know as much as me. All you can do is go for yourself. Did Barney play sax down here more than clarinet? I thought he started more on sax. Barney was playing a C melody saxophone. A C melody. That's right. And every job that Barney would get, all the best of clarinet players when they'd be out of a job, well they knew Barney was a weak man because he couldn't execute the clarinet like those guys was doing. So naturally they would go up there and see the man, whoever was the leader of the band, and he'd leave Barney go. Barney would come home, well I was single then. Barney would come home crying. So he said, mama, he said, well they called him Lorenzo, but they used to call him Big, they called him Big Eye Lou. He said, Big Eye Lou took my job. My grandma, my grandma, one reason one day because my mother, she died of childbirth, but he called my grandmother Mama. So she said, well why don't you give up? He said, no mama, I have to tell him. He said, I want to learn how to play the clarinet. So he'd go and get another job. My mother would be all bump. He'd come home crying. He says, my grandmother said, what's the matter now? He said, Piku took my job. My grandmother said, Barney, why don't you get yourself a job and go to work in the day? Give up. He says, no mother. He says, I'm deterrent. I'm deterrent. So he fooled around, he fooled around, he got another job. He was playing with Amos White. So finally, I know him twice. You heard him talk about that. Yes. He gets a job at Tom Anderson. And he had, he had, he had, she, Barbaran was playing the drum with her. He had Barney on tenor, C Melody at that time. And he had, Albert Nicholas was down here at that time. He had Albert Nicholas. And he had Udell on piano from St. Louis. And he had Willie Santiago on banjo. So, Barney told Arnold, he says, you know Arnold, he says, every time I get a job, he says, they take me, they turn around, they fire me and they take one of them stars. So Arnold said, well, you don't worry about it. He says, we're going to work a plan that you're going to be here. Well, I know I knew that Barney was a good musician, but he couldn't execute the clarinet like these other guys was doing around there. So Albert Nicholas was a fine clarinet player. So Albert and Barney, they got together and they made an arrangement that they would take and teach one another about the instrument. So Albert was never much of a reader, but Barney was the number one musician. So Barney said, well, Albert said, I'll tell you what I'll do with you. He said, if you learn me how to affect this clarinet, he says, I'll learn you the music. Well, they decided. Every day, I was working at the West End Bungalow at that time, and I used to sleep in the band there. I said, oh, for God's sake, get out of here with all that noise. And my grandmother said, well, he's got to learn, he's got to learn, he's got to learn. Yeah, he's got to learn. I said, well, wake me up. Let him go in the yard and play. And so finally they got together and they did turn out to be the best sacks team that they had around the city of New Orleans. And Barney then improved so much on that clarinet, he was getting great. So then Sidney Deadbeam was playing on the boat then, stealing a captain. Sidney tried to get them. He wanted the two of them. Well, though they wouldn't go. So T-Bob Barbran gets telegram from King Alba. King Alba wanted him to get some musicians from down there. So he got Alba Nicholas, he got Barney, Barney and him and they went to Chicago. Well, they joined King Alba's band up in Chicago. So when they joined King Alba's band in Chicago, Barney stood with them a long time. Then Duke Gelton drove over. And that's where Barney made a success. So when Barney came down here with Duke Gelton, first time Duke was down here, he had gave Duke a two weeks notice that he was leaving. So Big Alba and Pete Kool and fellas that was up there around the bandstand, giving Barney plenty of compliments the way he played clarinet. So Barney said, now look, he said, you know, y'all made me cry plenty. He said, y'all really made me cry. He says, now, he said, y'all got an opportunity. He says, Duke Gelton's down here right now. He needs a clarinet player. He said, yeah, want one of y'all up there, give him an audition. Probably take one of y'all. No, indeed, Barney, we ain't going behind you. No, indeed. He said, well, I'm sorry. He says, Duke got a two weeks notice. He said, now, if you want a job, he says, go up there, Duke, make an audition with Duke and Duke probably will hire. But they never, never do it. I was going to ask a little more about the violin player since you knew your uncle, of course, very well. How did he play? What kind of a part did they play? Oh, Monk, he was a good musician. He was a great musician. In fact, I think Monk was a better violin player than Pierron. But Pierron just had the name amongst the public. But to my estimation, he was better than Pierron. How was the old man Robichaud on violin? He was a- Well, he was never much of a violin player. But I tell you, he was a good musician. Good arranger and all. Yeah, good arranger. But he was never, I mean, it looked like you couldn't get no tone out of a violin like these other guys, you know. But uh, as far as arranging, as far as you, you the music. I don't care how many men you could have playing, you give everybody a part. You could tell what the man's not playing his part, what he's not making right, what he's making right, what he's not making right. He was a good director, a good musician, but he was never, not much of a violin player. Well, would he write out those arrangements himself? Oh yeah, yeah, yeah. You could hum a song and he, and he'd write it. Oh, he was great. He was great, but he was not much of a violin player. Couldn't execute it faster. Yeah. But he was wonderful. I'm wondering in the, say, the old time Dixieland type of music, you know, when they just fake, what kind of a part would the violin play? Would he stick right to the lead to playing like the trumpet part, or what did he do? Oh no, he'd fake it now, he'd fake it now. Would he play variations? Variations. Something like the clarinet, like a clarinet. Chords and all up and down. And it would sound good. It would sound real good. Would they harmonize with any other songs? Oh yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah, they would harmonize. Did he sometimes play a second part like down low maybe two or what? That's right. See, I never heard violin much. I heard Peter Boccage play the other night though. Yeah. On violin, he did very well too. Yeah. But I never heard much of the old time. How did he do it? And I'll tell you, sounds pretty good. Well, I'll tell you, in fact, not to say knocking, but the average band that we have around is not playing Dixieland music. No, that's right. Not like the old time, I bet. No, that's right. They're not playing. They're playing jazz. You see, Dixieland music can not be played fast, fast, fast, and see those guys playing some of these numbers. They got a swinging tempo. Two beats of them else, you see. Now, there you go. That, of course, that's the way you got to play with them today. They want you to do that. But that is supposed to be one beat. Dixieland is a one beat. Dixieland beat is not no two beat, but that's the way they want you to play today. You got to play the way they want you to play. Dixieland music is not no, there's not no 4-4-3. When did they start putting the 4-4 in? Oh, this year. Long time. Well, the original. The only time that we played 4-4 is when we was going out. See, like I tried explaining the fightless cymbal and the snare drum together. That's the only time we played a 4-4 when we were going out. But today, they want you to play a 4-4 beat all the way through.
